passages.label: READING PASSAGE 1

passages.title: Why Do People Go to University?
passages.subtitle: Exploring the value of a degree and alternative paths to a successful career
paragraphs: For many decades, going to university has been seen by parents and teachers as the main key to a successful life. After finishing high school, millions of young people around the world choose to spend three or four years studying for a university degree. The most common reason is to get better job opportunities. Many companies still ask for a university qualification before they will even invite a person to an interview.

In addition to getting a good job, people with a degree often earn a higher salary than people who start working straight after school. According to a recent report in the UK, university graduates earn an average of 20 percent more over their lifetime. For professions such as medicine, law, and engineering, a degree is not just helpful; it is a legal requirement. Without it, a person cannot legally work in those fields.

However, money and work are not the only reasons to study at university. Many students go because they have a strong interest in a specific subject and want to gain deeper knowledge. University libraries, laboratories, and experienced professors give students the chance to explore ideas in detail. Students also develop important soft skills, such as teamwork, time management, and critical thinking, which are useful in any future career.

University life also offers valuable social benefits. Moving away from home allows young adults to meet people from different cities and backgrounds. Joining student clubs, sports teams, or volunteer groups helps them build lasting friendships and a professional network that may support them later in life.

Despite these advantages, more young people today are asking whether university is really the best choice for everyone. In recent years, starting work or joining an apprenticeship straight after high school has become much more popular. Apprenticeships allow young people to learn practical skills on the job while earning a wage at the same time.

Some major technology and retail companies have even removed the need for a degree for many of their roles. Instead, they look at a candidate's experience, portfolio, and attitude. While a university education remains a strong path to success for many, experts agree that it is no longer the only way to build a rewarding career.

passages.title: Studying in Another Country
passages.subtitle: The rewards and realities of international education and student exchange programmes
paragraphs: A Every year, millions of students leave their home countries to take part in university courses or short-term student exchange programmes abroad. Studying in another country has become a common goal for young people who want to experience a new culture and improve their future career prospects. Universities around the world actively encourage this trend by offering international scholarships and partner programmes.

B According to Dr. Maya Patel, an education adviser in London, one of the greatest benefits of studying abroad is personal growth. 'When students move to a foreign city on their own, they have to manage their own budget, cook their own meals, and solve everyday problems,' she says. 'This forces them to become much more independent in a very short time.' She also notes that employers value international students because they can adapt quickly to unfamiliar situations.

C However, living far from home is not always easy. Tomoki Sato, a Japanese student who spent a year on an exchange programme in Australia, explains that the first few months were tough. 'Even though I studied English for years at school, I still faced a serious language barrier when people spoke fast or used local slang,' he remembers. 'I also felt very homesick during holidays and missed my family's cooking.' Fortunately, joining a local hiking club helped him make friends and feel more comfortable.

D Financial pressure is another major concern for international students. Apart from university fees, students must plan carefully for living costs such as rent, transport, and food, which can be much higher in major cities like London, New York, or Sydney. Elena Rossi, a financial counsellor at an international college, advises students to research local prices before they travel. 'Many students are surprised by how expensive accommodation is,' she says. 'Creating a clear monthly budget and checking whether their visa allows part-time work can prevent serious stress later.'

E Student exchange programmes, which usually last for one semester or one academic year, offer a popular alternative to completing a full degree overseas. Because exchange students normally pay fees to their home university, these short programmes are often cheaper and easier to arrange. Professor David Clark, who directs a university exchange office, believes that even a single semester abroad can change a student's worldview. 'Students return with greater confidence and a deeper respect for other traditions,' he explains.

F Despite the challenges, researchers agree that good preparation makes a big difference. Dr. Patel recommends that students learn basic phrases in the local language and connect with current students online before arriving. Meanwhile, Professor Clark suggests that universities should offer better orientation weeks and mental health support during the first term, so that newcomers do not feel isolated while adjusting to their new environment.

passages.title: Who Pays for University?
passages.subtitle: The global debate over tuition fees, student loans, and free higher education
paragraphs: Around the world, governments and families face a difficult question: who should pay for university education? While primary and secondary schools are free in almost every country, higher education is treated very differently. In some nations, students pay thousands of dollars every year in tuition fees, whereas in others, university is completely free. Both systems have strong supporters and loud critics.

In countries like Germany, Norway, and Finland, the government pays for public universities using money collected from taxes. Supporters of free education argue that access to university should depend on a student's ability and hard work, not on how rich their parents are. When tuition fees are removed, young people from low-income families can afford to study medicine, science, or teaching. Supporters also believe that a better-educated population benefits the whole society by creating more skilled workers and a stronger economy.

However, providing free university education is not without problems. Running modern universities with good libraries, up-to-date technology, and well-paid teachers is extremely expensive. Critics point out that when universities are funded only by the government, public money may be taken away from other essential services such as hospitals or primary schools. Furthermore, some economists argue that free tuition is actually unfair to taxpayers who never went to university themselves, because their taxes help pay for graduates who will later earn high incomes.

On the other hand, countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia charge significant tuition fees. To help students who cannot pay upfront, these countries offer a student loan system. Under this system, students borrow money to cover their fees and only start paying it back after they graduate and earn above a certain income level. Supporters claim that this approach brings more funding into universities, allowing them to improve research facilities and attract top professors.

Nevertheless, the loan system also creates serious worries. In many cases, graduates leave university with large debts that take decades to repay. Fear of debt can discourage students from poorer backgrounds from applying to university in the first place. It can also push graduates to choose high-paying jobs in finance or business instead of lower-paid but socially important careers such as social work or public teaching.

Because neither system is perfect, many education experts now suggest a middle path. They believe governments should charge moderate tuition fees for wealthier families while offering full grants and scholarships to students who cannot afford to pay. In my view, this balanced model is the most practical solution: it keeps universities well funded without blocking talented young people from getting a degree simply because of their family's income.
